candidato.titulo: STAT+: Pharmalittle: We’re reading about a Roche lung cancer drug, a Bristol CAR-T trial death, and more
candidato.resumo: Bristol Myers Squibb reported that one patient died after receiving its investigational CAR-T therapy in an early autoimmune trial

texto_fonte:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to another working week. We hope the weekend respite was relaxing and invigorating because that oh-too-familiar routine of meetings, deadlines, and the like has returned with a vengeance. But what can you do? The world, such as it is, continues to rotate. To nudge it in a better direction, we are brewing another cup of stimulation. Our choice today is butter pecan with a dash of raw honey. Feel free to join us. Remember, no prescription is required. Meanwhile, here are some tidbits to help you along. Best of luck accomplishing your goals today, and of course, do keep in touch. …
Bristol Myers Squibb reported that one patient died after receiving its investigational CAR-T therapy in an early autoimmune trial, adding to safety concerns about a growing field of research, STAT notes. In a Phase 1 trial that tested the therapy in multiple sclerosis, the patient experienced motor symptoms that did not resolve with standard autoimmune treatments. They were then given a potent immunosuppressant, but developed septic pneumonia and died, Bristol said in a press release. In a subsequent statement, Bristol said this patient was treated for a series of other complications prior to receiving the CAR-T therapy, “confounding our ability to determine the root cause of the issue.”
A Roche drug billed as a potential blockbuster helped patients with a form of lung cancer that had spread live almost six months longer than two competitive medicines, Bloomberg News says. The experimental treatment, called divarasib, fared better than similar drugs from Amgen and Bristol Myers Squibb in a late-stage study. The drug was given to patients with non-small cell lung cancer that had spread, in part because of a genetic mutation, after other treatments, including chemotherapy. The findings could help divarasib become the treatment of choice for this type of lung cancer, in which a mutation called KRAS G12C drives the tumor cell growth.

candidato.titulo: Protein fibers, a hallmark of Alzheimer's, spotted making genetic deliveries to sperm cells
candidato.resumo: Unexpectedly, a kind of protein that is usually linked with diseases in the brain may play a vital role in semen, helping shepherd genetic material into sperm cells, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute report in the journal Molecular Cell.

texto_fonte:
Protein fibers, a hallmark of Alzheimer's, spotted making genetic deliveries to sperm cells
Unexpectedly, a kind of protein that is usually linked with diseases in the brain may play a vital role in semen, helping shepherd genetic material into sperm cells, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute report in the journal Molecular Cell.
These findings raise the possibility that these proteins, known as amyloids, may one day help improve gene-editing technologies such as CRISPR.
"This is wild biology," said senior author on the paper Anthony Fitzpatrick, Ph.D., a principal investigator at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute. "Amyloids are most often thought of as a hallmark of Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and other neurodegenerative diseases in the brain, but they also have functional roles throughout the body and keep turning up in unexpected places."
An HIV clue points to RNA
This unusual project had an even more unusual starting point: the virus HIV. Previous research had found that amyloid fibrils present in semen could help HIV enter cells in the reproductive tract, explained William Mallen, Ph.D., the study's lead author, who conducted this research while he was a doctoral student in the Fitzpatrick lab.
Fitzpatrick, an expert on amyloids in brain research, wondered if those fibrils could also help materials naturally in the body enter sperm: specifically, the genetic molecule RNA, which helps turn instructions encoded in DNA into protein molecules.
Scientists knew that seminal fluid contains lots of small RNAs, thought to play a major role in what genes are active in developing embryos. But how this RNA gets chaperoned from seminal fluid into sperm to influence the embryo—that was a mystery.
The potential link the researchers made between amyloids and RNA was how HIV uses RNA as its genetic material, as is true with roughly half of all known viruses. Since amyloids could help HIV enter cells, maybe they could do so with RNA in general.
Amyloids seemed promising escorts for RNA, in part because these amyloids are positively charged, while RNA is negatively charged, and for molecules, like magnets, opposites attract.
Using fluorescent labels on both kinds of molecules, Mallen found that they do bind together and speculated that the amyloids have a protective function. While RNA is quite fragile, amyloids are exceptionally durable, so packaging RNA in an amyloid scaffold could help the genetic molecules survive harsh conditions.
Imaging confirms amyloids enter sperm
The researchers next analyzed sperm using cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), which fires beams of electrons at frozen specimens to create 3D images of the samples.
Cryo-ET, the most powerful form of microscopy used in biology today, can achieve near-atomic-level resolution. Using amyloid proteins labeled with flecks of gold, the scientists confirmed these molecules could in fact enter sperm, and not just, say, embed onto their surfaces.
"Seeing those amyloid fibers inside sperm cells was just so extraordinary to me," said Mallen, who is now in medical school at the University of Vermont. "There were hints of this happening earlier in our other experiments, but actually seeing this just totally blew us away."
In addition, the researchers used a fluorescent protein to assess the rate at which RNA entered the sperm and found that amyloids could greatly enhance that. Once RNA that was bound to amyloid made its way into cells, a protein known as clusterin could help separate RNA from amyloid.
"It's a seminal discovery," Fitzpatrick said. All in all, he said they were a testament to Mallen, "a fearless graduate student willing to pursue real swing-for-the-fences type of science." Mallen noted that at the Fitzpatrick lab, "everything is 'go big or go home.'"
Questions about inherited gene activity
While the researchers do not yet know what the amyloid-shuttled RNA does once inside the sperm, previous research found that RNA in semen can switch genes on or off in offspring. These epigenetic modifications can be shaped by a parent's experiences and be inherited from generation to generation.
"There are metabolic disorders such as insulin resistance that recent papers have shown can be passed down the paternal line in mice, and it's thought RNA is how," Mallen said. "By learning how disorders based on epigenetics work, we can come closer to how to possibly treat or prevent them."
Potential delivery tools for gene editing
The researchers also suggest that amyloids might one day serve as tools to deliver RNA into cells. For instance, the gene-editing technology known as CRISPR, which uses RNA, has triggered a revolution in genetics for how it can help scientists modify genes in a cheap, fast and easy way, with hundreds of clinical trials currently testing how CRISPR might find use in gene therapies.
In experiments, amyloid fibrils could bring not only small RNAs into sperm but also RNA molecules large enough to encode a green fluorescent protein. Embryos fertilized using this sperm could generate at least 10 times more of this protein than sperm exposed to this RNA without the amyloids. These findings suggest that scientists could one day use amyloids to, say, shuttle therapeutic genes into cells and embryos.
The researchers noted that CRISPR often currently relies on modified viruses as a delivery mechanism, which can trigger immune reactions.
"Since the amyloid fibrils we looked at are human-based, hopefully the immune system won't react in the same way it does to the repurposed viruses often used in gene therapy," Mallen said.
Publication details
Amyloid-mediated RNA uptake by sperm for embryonic delivery, Molecular Cell (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.molcel.2026.10.004. www.cell.com/molecular-cell/fu … 1097-2765(26)00709-4

texto_fonte:
Rival da BYD apresenta novos SUVs híbridos com IA e foco off-road
Por Danielle Cassita | •
A chinesa Jetour reuniu milhares de convidados em Wuhu, na China, para apresentar seus novos modelos e inovações para o futuro da mobilidade no Jetour Global Technology Experience Day. Durante o evento, a marca do grupo Chery trouxe aplicações de inteligência artificial, robótica e novas arquiteturas veiculares que devem equipar os futuros lançamentos do grupo — incluindo mercados internacionais, como o Brasil.
Na prática, o encontro foi como uma vitrine para a ofensiva tecnológica da montadora, que quer oferecer soluções de recarga bidirecional (V2G), ecossistemas de energia solar integrados e projetos de condução autônoma com frotas de Robotaxis desenvolvidas em parceria com a AiMOGA Robotics.
O destaque automotivo ficou por conta da evolução das famílias de SUVs T e G, focadas em alto desempenho fora de estrada sem abrir mão do conforto para o uso urbano. A série T, por exemplo, aposta no sistema híbrido C-DM Super Hybrid combinado à tração integral inteligente XWD, além de modos de condução off-road programáveis com gerenciamento eletrônico ativo.
Lançamentos da Jetour
A série G, por sua vez, adota como pilar a nova arquitetura GAIA, desenvolvida sob medida para encarar diferentes tipos de terreno. A base estrutural incorpora chassis reforçados para o off-road pesado, sistemas híbridos de alta eficiência energética, acabamento de padrão premium na cabine e recursos avançados de conectividade interativa.
Yin Tongyue, o presidente da Chery, ressaltou o papel central da inteligência artificial como o motor transformador do grupo, que já soma mais de 30 anos de inovação, para as próximas etapas. Com o plano de acelerar a eletrificação e a conectividade, as soluções apresentadas na China devem começar a ser repassadas gradualmente para o portfólio global de produtos das marcas do grupo Chery.

candidato.titulo: Microsoft amplia prazo para encontrar comprador da Arkane Lyon, estúdio de Marvel’s Blade
candidato.resumo: Responsável por Dishonored e Deathloop, desenvolvedora francesa enfrenta risco de fechamento enquanto continua trabalhando no jogo do caçador de vampiros da Marvel O post Microsoft amplia prazo para encontrar comprador da Arkane Lyon, estúdio de Marvel’s Blade apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

texto_fonte:
A Microsoft decidiu ampliar em um mês o período de consultas sobre o futuro da Arkane Lyon, estúdio francês responsável pelo desenvolvimento de Marvel’s Blade. A empresa busca um comprador ou parceiro que permita a continuidade das atividades da desenvolvedora, ameaçada de fechamento durante a reestruturação da divisão Xbox.
Segundo informações do GamesIndustry.biz, o processo estava inicialmente previsto para terminar em 13 de novembro de 2026, mas recebeu uma extensão enquanto as negociações continuam.
Um representante da Microsoft confirmou a prorrogação ao PC Gamer, afirmando que a companhia continuará mantendo os representantes dos trabalhadores informados durante o processo.
Arkane Lyon pode ser vendida para evitar fechamento
A situação da Arkane Lyon começou a se agravar em julho, quando a Microsoft anunciou planos para se desfazer de cinco estúdios como parte de uma reestruturação da divisão de games.
Desde então, a empresa negocia com o Comitê Social e Econômico da Arkane, órgão francês responsável pela representação dos funcionários.
De acordo com o jornal francês Le Monde, diferentes possibilidades de aquisição estão sendo consideradas. Entretanto, um documento interno consultado pela publicação aponta que o encerramento definitivo das atividades também permanece entre os cenários possíveis.
Nesse caso, o processo de fechamento poderia começar no final de 2026 e se estender até o primeiro trimestre de 2027.
A situação preocupa os funcionários. Um representante do sindicato Printemps Écologique afirmou ao Le Monde que as negociações sobre possíveis demissões enfrentam dificuldades e questionou a decisão de vender um estúdio que, segundo os representantes dos trabalhadores, apresenta bons resultados.
A reportagem também menciona que 217 empregos estão ameaçados.
O que acontece com Marvel’s Blade?
Apesar das incertezas sobre o futuro da Arkane Lyon, o desenvolvimento de Marvel’s Blade continua.
Em declaração enviada à IGN, a Microsoft afirmou que está avaliando alternativas para o estúdio e procurando um parceiro capaz de apoiar a próxima etapa de produção e a comercialização do jogo.
Isso significa que o projeto não foi oficialmente cancelado, mas seu futuro depende do resultado das negociações.
Anunciado em 2023, Marvel’s Blade é um jogo de ação em terceira pessoa protagonizado pelo caçador de vampiros da Marvel. O título está sendo desenvolvido pela Arkane Lyon, conhecida por Dishonored 2 e Deathloop.
Por enquanto, a Microsoft não anunciou um comprador, nem esclareceu como uma eventual venda afetaria os direitos de desenvolvimento e publicação do jogo.
Com a extensão do prazo, a Arkane Lyon ganha mais tempo para encontrar uma solução que permita a continuidade do estúdio e de Marvel’s Blade.

candidato.titulo: Intel's Lip-Bu Tan has spoken with Lisa Su about potential collaboration with AMD
candidato.resumo: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has reportedly discussed potential areas of cooperation with AMD chief Lisa Su as Intel works to rebuild its CPU business and expand its foundry operations. The companies have already collaborated on x86 standards and CPU software, including AMD’s integration of its ZenDNN optimizations into Intel’s oneDNN library. Neither executive has publicly detailed the reported discussions or confirmed a new agreement.

texto_fonte:
Intel and AMD have spent decades competing for the processors inside PCs and data centers, but the rivalry hasn't stopped the two companies from working together when their interests align. And now, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has reportedly discussed potential areas of cooperation with AMD chief Lisa Su, adding another possible partnership to the mix as Intel tries to regain its footing in the semiconductor industry.
According to a recording (embedded below) of Tan’s October 24 fireside chat with Chinese American Semiconductor Professional Association (CASPA) President Jimmy Cheng, the Intel CEO outlined his plans to rebuild the company’s CPU business, develop chips tailored to specific customer workloads, and attract more customers to its foundry operations. However, Tan did not publicly detail the reported areas of potential cooperation with AMD CEO Lisa Su.
Intel has traditionally built its business around its own processor roadmaps, but Tan says the company needs to be more flexible as customers look for silicon designed for particular workloads. He pointed to Intel's Xeon processors as one area where that approach is changing, alongside continued development of GPUs and accelerators.
"We have to reclaim the leadership in CPU. That is something that I am very determined to do." Tan said.
He also described a change in how Intel approaches customization. "Intel is so proud they never want to modify for customer needs," he said. "I'm modifying it for customer needs, and so that, I think, to me, is a fast-growing area, and I'm double, triple down on it."
The strategy extends beyond conventional CPUs, with Tan identifying application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), co-packaged optics (CPO), physical AI, and advanced packaging as potential growth businesses. He wants two or three of these areas to eventually contribute around 10% of Intel's revenue each.
Intel's foundry business is another major part of Tan's plans. He said the company's 18A manufacturing process had reached volume production, while development of its next-generation 14A process was progressing strongly. Intel has already released version 0.5 of the 14A process design kit (PDK), which provides chip designers with the technical information and tools needed to develop products for the process.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Tan said version 0.9 was coming next, followed by version 1.0 for volume production in early 2027. "We have multiple customers [who] really want us to really scale their business," he said, referring to interest in Intel's foundry services.
However, Intel did not identify those customers or disclose the size of any potential manufacturing orders during the discussion. Notably, in January, Intel had two prospective customers evaluating 14A test chips, with firm supplier decisions expected during the second half of 2026 and the first half of 2027. Tan also described foundry manufacturing as a business where trust matters as much as technology. Customers hand over wafers that will eventually become products on which their own revenue depends, making missed deadlines or manufacturing problems costly. "The moment we take on the foundry, take on the wafer is a lot of responsibility to make them successful," he said.
He recalled one customer who had waited six to eight months hoping he would become CEO before presenting 15 areas where Intel had fallen short. Tan said he addressed the problems individually, after which the customer agreed to deepen its relationship with Intel.
That said, the prospect of further cooperation would not be entirely new. In October 2024, Intel and AMD established the x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group alongside other technology companies to coordinate improvements to the x86 instruction set architecture and make it easier for hardware and software developers to support both companies' processors.
That cooperation has since moved into AI software. Last week, it emerged that AMD was integrating its ZenDNN optimizations into Intel's open-source oneDNN library, bringing the companies' CPU optimization work for PyTorch AI inference under a common software path. The companies have also worked together on Advanced Matrix Extensions and other x86 capabilities through the advisory group, showing that they cooperate on shared technologies while continuing to compete for customers. For now, however, neither company has announced a new agreement arising from the discussions.

candidato.titulo: Stellar collisions may have been common when the universe was young
candidato.resumo: In our solar system's corner of the galaxy, stars rarely collide. It makes sense: Space is vast, and stars have room to roam. Even in most of the present-day universe, stellar collisions are rare. The James Webb Space Telescope, however, peers deep enough into space to see the universe as it was not too long after the Big Bang. Its observations have revealed extraordinarily compact stellar systems, raising the possibility that collisions between stars were once much more common.

texto_fonte:
Stellar collisions may have been common when the universe was young
In our solar system's corner of the galaxy, stars rarely collide. It makes sense: Space is vast, and stars have room to roam. Even in most of the present-day universe, stellar collisions are rare. The James Webb Space Telescope, however, peers deep enough into space to see the universe as it was not too long after the Big Bang. Its observations have revealed extraordinarily compact stellar systems, raising the possibility that collisions between stars were once much more common.
A new study—led by UCLA astrophysicists and currently published on the arXiv preprint server—finds that in the early universe, stellar systems were extremely dense, with stars frequently hitting each other. These collisions could happen at either very rapid speeds, which destroyed the stars, or more slowly, in which case they merged into one.
Stellar mergers build black hole seeds
Repeated mergers could produce a single extraordinarily massive star, which might eventually collapse into a black hole. Some of these gigantic stars eventually became black holes. The finding could help explain how the seeds of supermassive black holes formed early enough to grow into the enormous black holes already present in the young universe.
"Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster," said UCLA doctoral student and corresponding author Claire Williams. "When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole."
The center of the Milky Way provides a nearby example of the same basic ingredients: a massive black hole embedded within a dense nuclear star cluster. The model suggests that once a black hole is present, its gravity accelerates nearby stars, causing collisions close to the black hole to destroy them rather than merge them and release gas into the surrounding region.
"One place in the nearby universe where collisions between stars are common is the galactic center," Williams said. "In our model, once these very massive stars turn into intermediate-mass black holes, the system resembles our own galactic center, which is a black hole surrounded by a dense star cluster."
Connecting the little red dots
The origin of supermassive black holes has been a mystery. Astronomers expected they would grow gradually, but the James Webb Space Telescope has found them forming quickly after the Big Bang. The new research is not the first to propose stellar collisions as the mechanism, but the modeling ties together observations, such as intriguing "little red dots" (LRDs), and theoretical models to identify clear pathways to collisions for stars within dense clusters and the formation of supermassive black holes.
LRDs—extremely compact objects in the early universe that look like red dots—are believed to contain a rapidly growing black hole at the center. The new simulations suggest that LRDs may be dense star clusters filled with stellar collisions that are forming a very large star, which may eventually become a black hole.
"Little red dots are a hot topic in astronomy. You can compare studies of people trying to understand LRDs to the tale of blind people who are trying to describe an elephant by touching it, and each person describes it differently based on what part they're touching," UCLA astrophysicist and co-author Smadar Naoz said. "Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant."
Dense clusters in a young universe
Intermediate-mass black holes may need a cluster like this in order to exist. These are an elusive type of black hole—larger than those that form when a star dies, but smaller than the supermassive black holes that dominate the centers of galaxies. They are almost never observed.
The clusters originate from conditions unique to the early universe, which was very different from what we see today. There were no big spiral galaxies like the Milky Way, just regions with dense clusters of star formation. Within these clusters, stars were colliding and forming black holes, around which galaxies would eventually form. Eventually, the universe expanded, became less extreme and moved toward the equilibrium state it is in now.
"Dense star clusters provide a natural birthplace for massive black-hole seeds in our model," Williams said. "The same environment that forms the black hole can also provide stars and gas that influence its subsequent growth."
Publication details
Claire E. Williams et al., A cosmological framework for stellar collisions at high redshift in proto-globular clusters, nuclear star clusters, and Little Red Dots, arXiv (2026). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2603.26872

candidato.titulo: Quantum Art Research Outlines More Efficient Quantum Approach to Wave Modeling
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — – Quantum Art, a developer of full-stack, fault tolerant quantum computers based on trapped-ion qubits and a proprietary, dynamically reconfigurable multi-core architecture, recently presented new research, detailed in this paper, that solves wave-propagation problems long thought intractable for classical supercomputers – unlocking new simulation capabilities for seismic modeling, structural engineering, […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- Quantum Art presented research on a quantum algorithm that uses known wave physics to simplify large-scale wave simulations, with potential applications in telecommunications, seismic modeling and engineering.
- The method constructs physically allowed wave states directly, aiming to avoid computational overhead that limits existing quantum approaches as the modeled region grows.
- The company estimates that some simulations requiring 10¹⁸–10²¹ classical grid points could potentially use roughly 100 qubits, although practical implementation depends on further hardware advances.
PRESS RELEASE — – Quantum Art, a developer of full-stack, fault tolerant quantum computers based on trapped-ion qubits and a proprietary, dynamically reconfigurable multi-core architecture, recently presented new research, detailed in this paper, that solves wave-propagation problems long thought intractable for classical supercomputers – unlocking new simulation capabilities for seismic modeling, structural engineering, and materials science.
Simulating how waves, from radio signals to sound, travel through space demands enormous computing power, and that demand grows sharply when the area being modeled gets larger but the level of detail cannot be reduced. The stakes are real for industries that depend on precision: telecom carriers predict network coverage, engineers model how buildings and materials hold up under stress, and geophysicists track how seismic waves move through the earth. The research explains the science behind the large-scale wave-simulation results the company previously demonstrated in May through a joint project with a leading Israeli governmental research and development agency.
Quantum computers hold a key advantage here: they can represent extremely large problems using relatively few qubits. Most existing quantum methods, however, treat a wave problem as a vast, generic mathematical puzzle. They solve a huge system of equations by brute force, with little regard for what the equations describe. Waves follow strict physical rules: a wave of a given frequency travels at a fixed speed in a given medium, so every direction it could possibly travel in can be pictured as the hand of a clock. Because the speed is fixed, every hand is the same length, so their tips can only trace out one perfect circle. Anything off that circle is physically impossible. Prior methods still expend effort searching far outside that circle, checking possibilities that the physics has already ruled out. As a result, they tend to slow dramatically or lose their quantum advantage, especially on a large-scale problem.
Quantum Art’s new approach turns known wave physics into a shortcut. Rather than asking the quantum computer to solve the full mathematical puzzle, it directly builds that circle of physically allowed wave directions and marks the location of each wave source on it. The answer is constructed from the known shape of wave physics instead of being calculated from scratch. It is the difference between searching an entire library page by page and walking straight to the one shelf where the book is known to be.
The approach reflects a pattern that runs through Quantum Art’s work more broadly: the company again uses physics itself to shorten the path toward practical quantum computing. The same philosophy shapes its hardware, where trapped-ion qubits, multi-qubit gates, and a dynamically reconfigurable multi-core architecture are built around the physical behavior of the system rather than engineered around it.
Amit Ben Kish, Chief Technology Officer at Quantum Art, said, “This paper explains the underlying science behind our approach and shows it is not limited to radio and electromagnetic signals. The same principle applies to any wave governed by a fixed relationship between frequency and speed, which opens the door to simulating problems in sound, radar, and seismic wave propagation.”
Until now, quantum approaches to these problems have run into a wall. Some require running the quantum computer for longer and longer stretches as the simulated area grows. Others, which search the full mathematical space and keep only the useful part, succeed so rarely on large problems that they would need to be repeated an extraordinary number of times. Either way, the quantum advantage erodes as the modeled regions get larger.
Quantum Art’s new method removes that wall. Because it builds only the part of the answer that matters, the number of attempts required stays roughly the same whether the simulated area is the size of a room or a mountain range, and computational effort grows only slowly as the simulation becomes more detailed. Its chances of success even improve as more wave sources are involved. A detailed, three-dimensional simulation of radio waves spanning tens of kilometers, accurate to the centimeter, can require 10¹⁸-10²¹ classical grid points – a scale that is far beyond what even today’s largest supercomputers can practically handle, yet potentially within reach of a quantum computer with on the order of 100 qubits. Reaching that scale in practice will also build on continued hardware progress, including Quantum Art’s multi-qubit gates, which compress circuit depth and reduce the error introduced as systems scale up.
For the first time, this makes it plausible for a quantum computer to efficiently model steady wave patterns (i.e., sound, radar, or seismic waves at a fixed frequency) across regions far larger than any classical computer could handle.
Matt Swayne

texto_fonte:
Right now you can buy a new laptop powered by an Nvidia processor. That would have been a wild statement a few years ago. But what’s even wilder is that these RTX Spark laptops aren’t for PC gamers, and PC gamers shouldn’t buy them.
That’s not to say they’re bad. The RTX Spark platform is impressive, even if it’s currently going through a bit of a teething phase. It’s phenomenally powerful, a true Windows alternative to Apple’s Arm chips. And of course it’s great at just about anything having to do with local “AI,” as that’s its primary purpose. For more info on that, check out Mark Hachman’s full review of the Surface Laptop Ultra, on the same platform.
But when most people think of an “Nvidia laptop,” they probably assume it’s for gaming. And the RTX Spark can do gaming. Quite a lot of gaming, in fact — the pre-release estimate that the integrated graphics run at “5070 level” is approximately on the money. I’ve found the initial testing on HP’s $3199 Omnibook 16 Ultra impressive, extremely so for integrated graphics.
Unfortunately, the price of these RTX Spark laptops — ranging from $2600 to $7000 at launch — simply makes them a poor proposition for anyone primarily interested in gaming. You’re paying a massive premium for the level of gaming performance you get, starting at about a thousand dollars more than an equivalent laptop with a discrete graphics card, and only going up from there.
Asus
The RTX Spark is amazing. We didn’t need proof that integrated graphics could handle impressive gaming, not with the last few years of handhelds demonstrating it. But Nvidia may have proven that you can do it on Arm just as well, possibly better, than X64 chips. But you won’t be doing it on a budget, at least not with the initial chips and laptop designs.
Compatibility issues, or lack thereof
One of the potential problems that cropped up with early Arm-based chips from Qualcomm going into Windows laptops was basic app compatibility. Windows users remember the problems with Windows RT… or perhaps I should say, one of the problems with Windows RT. But in the time since, and the rise of smartphones and other devices based on Arm chips, those seem to have largely been handled. I’d have no problem recommending an Arm laptop to anyone, especially if they prized battery life over power.
The big exception is gamers. Snapdragon laptops are, plainly, kinda crap at PC games, only handling older 2D titles with any deftness. So I was interested to see how Nvidia would handle this, since as a brand it’s intimately associated with PC games. In the lead-up to the RTX Spark launch, the company promised powerful games and “hundreds” of titles compatible right off the bat, prepared in cooperation with some of the biggest publishers and developers in the industry.
Michael Crider/Foundry
And not much else. If anything, Nvidia is being a little reticent with its gaming talk for these laptops, preferring to talk about core power and AI capabilities. It lets you know where the priorities are.
But anyway. If you’re worried about compatibility for RTX Spark laptops, you shouldn’t be. I tried to throw every curveball I could at the Omnibook, including visually spectacular titles like Space Marine II, brand new games (presumably without much testing on the new chips) like Galactic Racer, 2D games like Absolum, and positively ancient stuff from the deepest, darkest part of my Steam library.
The laptop installed and ran very nearly all of them without any issues at all. I ran into two notable problems: the original release of Skyrim (11/11/11, or if you’re outside the United States, 11/11/11) refused to launch. The remastered PC version from 2021 ran fine. I also couldn’t run the demo for Shadow of the Tomb Raider, a bit of a bummer since it has a good benchmark…but I’ve honestly never played it for myself. The only other issue I encountered was with Mount & Blade: Warband, a small but tricky DirectX9 game from 2010. It ran, but at about a quarter of the framerate I was expecting based on the other games I tried.
Michael Crider/Foundry
Everything else was fine. I was expecting to encounter far more problems, since PC game developers have never had any serious push to make Windows-compatible titles run well on Arm. Whatever else its priorities might be, Nvidia (with Microsoft’s likely help) has to be commended for nailing the game compatibility right at launch.
Performance is good…but not incredible
The Omnibook Ultra makes a good gaming laptop. With those compatibility concerns put aside, I was shocked at how well it handled all the games I threw at it. In short, yeah, it handles modern games of all stripes at about the same level as a laptop sporting a discrete RTX 5070 card… maybe a little less.
As it happens, PCWorld just published a gaming laptop review with a discrete RTX 5070 card, the MSI Stealth 16 AI+. That’s a conventional design with a Core Ultra 9 processor and 32GB of RAM, though it should be pointed out that with an integrated setup, the RTX Spark has to share system and GPU memory. Even so it was an opportunity for a very relevant head-to-head showdown.
The HP laptop with RTX Spark managed to beat the discrete GPU machine on Geekbench 7’s GPU test by a 5 percent margin, 113022 to 107232. On the CPU side in the same tool it was less powerful than the Core Ultra 9 386H, in single-core mode, 2143 to 2560. But it pulled ahead in multi-core by flexing those 20 Grace cores, 19599 to 15503. For more traditional graphics tests, I took a look at standardized 3DMark. Results were mixed, with RTX Spark unsurprisingly performing better on tests that had native Arm versions (Steel Nomad and Port Royal).
I’m guessing that the Spark is slightly hobbled in these tests by sharing memory between the system and GPU, but getting a boost on the ray tracing test thanks to some extra work put in by Nvidia on the newer chip. Suffice it to say, even if it’s not beating the RTX 5070 in most pure tests, it’s certainly within the ballpark.
For standard game benchmarks, I pulled out a different laptop that I happened to have handy, so I could make sure the variables in the benchmarks were exact. A Razer Blade 18 with a Core i9-13950HX, and a last-gen RTX 4080 (12GB VRAM on the laptop version of the card) should be fairly evenly-matched with this newer laptop, at least if we take Nvidia’s “5070” claims at face value. I’ll add for the sake of comparison that this laptop cost $3800 when it launched in 2023, and buying a new laptop with this GPU and approximately matching specs today would cost about $2500.
I normalized the tests on high settings, 1080p, fullscreen. For Cyberpunk I also added a ray tracing test, just to see if the newer chip has an advantage.
So yeah, this RTX Spark laptop is getting pretty thoroughly beaten in gaming performance by a 3-year-old laptop with a 13th-gen Intel processor. Those aren’t easily available to buy anymore, but comparable prices on newer laptops aren’t favorable here, as you’ll see in the next section. You can make up the difference with a lot of frame generation…but unless you’re using 5x or 6x a lot, you’re not going to beat it.
While that display isn’t as big or as fast as the most bombastic gaming laptops on the market, it’s more than serviceable, and better than many that stick to LED panels. You might not like the glossy finish, but that’s just standard for non-gaming laptops. The keyboard is also pretty darn good, which is more than you can say for at least some of these initial RTX Spark designs. Naturally if you don’t like either you can plug it into any monitor you like. Using both HDMI and USB-C and connecting it to 5K displays it showed no issues.
Michael Crider/Foundry
That said, with a big, thirsty 99.9 watt-hour battery, you might not be able to get this thing to plug into even a gaming monitor with a single cable. At least not for long. Running through benchmarks on battery, just to see how long I could push it, the laptop blasted through the maximum size allowed on an airliner in just about an hour flat. It looks like even Nvidia can’t design a chip that combines gaming power with endurance.
The HP laptop comes with 32GB of RAM at this, its base level. The Spark laptops have up to 128GB of memory, which is what pushes those prices towards used car territory. So you might be wondering if all that extra memory — shared dynamically between the GPU the system, as with AMD’s high-powered chips with integrated graphics — can be put to use in games. I wondered too. Gosh, aren’t we both clever?
Brad Chacos/Foundry
The answer is, apparently, no. I asked Brad Chacos to run identical benchmarks on his Asus laptop, with four times the RAM. They came out with no statistical differences. There might be Spark laptops that run the same tests with worse performance — some of the less ridiculously expensive variants come with “only” 24GB of memory, which again, has to be shared between system and graphics. But from a gaming perspective, it won’t benefit you to splash out on 48GB, 64GB, or 128GB, at least not without games that are specifically designed to take advantage of an unreasonable amount of memory.
It’s possible that Nvidia could substantially improve the gaming performance in a short amount of time after launch. We saw the same thing happen when Intel debuted its own discrete graphics cards, and some quick driver tuning improved things markedly. But presumably Nvidia has already put as much time and money into this as it thinks is prudent. So I think it’s also possible that the only major boosts in performance come from the developer side of things, at least in the short term. But really, virtually no games require anywhere near the sort of massive memory pool available in RTX Spark laptops. It’s overkill.
The price is the problem
HP wants $3200 for the Omnibook 16 Ultra. Even in the nightmare that is laptop shopping in 2026, that is a lot of money. (And a lot of money to spend on a laptop that’s still pre-loaded with McAfee bloatware, but that’s another article.) More pertinently, it’s at least a thousand bucks more than you should spend for a laptop with this level of gaming performance.
Doing some online shopping in mid-October — because these things are, sadly, in constant flux — I found similarly-equipped laptops with a discrete RTX 5070, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD for a little above the $2000 mark. Some are a little more, particularly if you’re looking for a nice OLED screen. The MSI compared above is $2300. Some are significantly less, like this Gigabyte Aero X16, going for under $1800 when I checked.
Amazon
The laptop with a discrete card is big and chunky. It’s thicker than the HP despite having a smaller battery. But it’s actually lighter, 1.9kg/4.2 pounds versus 2.2kg/4.9 pounds for the HP. Again, the battery is probably part of that, plus a nice sleek metal chassis.
I can’t speak for everyone. But if I’m looking for a laptop primarily to play games, and knowing I’m going to be using a mouse, keyboard, and external monitor a lot the time, I can forgive a little bulk for $1500 in savings. That’s enough to buy a very nice monitor, after all. If you take it in the other direction, you could get a laptop with considerably more graphical power for the same price.
Who is the RTX Spark for?
So yeah, this laptop and its stablemates aren’t for gamers. Or at least, they’re not for gamers who are looking for a good value. If you want a laptop that can play plenty of games and be thin, and possibly even light if you go for a smaller screen, that might do it.
It might make sense if you’re already in the market for a beefy, powerful laptop for other purposes — running local AI agents, naturally, but possibly other workstation-class uses — and see the gaming prowess as icing on the cake. That would make the RTX Spark a true and compelling alternative to Macbook Pro, at least at some configurations…though it’s worth noting that Apple’s chips are still blazing fast at single-core performance.
Mark Hachman / Foundry
So you could see the gaming capabilities of these RTX Spark laptops as the icing on the cake. An expensive cake, with multiple tiers, and probably baked by someone with lots of accents in their name. It’s a definite bonus, and I could see it swaying some buyers away from a MacBook Pro.
But for gamers, and gamers without an unlimited budget? No, stick with conventional gaming laptops. The future looks bright for integrated graphics and PC gaming on Arm. But at the moment, it’s also a long way away.

texto_fonte:
Elvis vs. IA: donos dos direitos do Rei do Rock processam dona do Claude; entenda motivo
Por Marcelo Fischer |
Os responsáveis pelos direitos autorais de 274 músicas gravadas por Elvis Presley entraram com um processo contra a Anthropic, desenvolvedora da inteligência artificial (IA) Claude. A ação, apresentada na sexta-feira (23) nos Estados Unidos, acusa a empresa de utilizar as composições sem autorização para treinar seus modelos e pede uma indenização que pode chegar a US$ 48,6 milhões (cerca de R$ 242 milhões).
Entre as músicas envolvidas estão clássicos do Rei do Rock, como "Can't Help Falling in Love", "Don't Be Cruel", "All Shook Up", "Return to Sender" e "A Little Less Conversation".
Segundo a revista Billboard, a ação foi apresentada por uma subsidiária da Authentic Brands Group, empresa que administra parte dos direitos associados a Elvis Presley, além de editoras musicais e representantes de compositores.
O processo tramita em um tribunal federal da Califórnia e busca responsabilizar a Anthropic pelo suposto uso indevido das obras.
Por que os donos das músicas de Elvis processaram a Anthropic?
De acordo com a acusação, a Anthropic teria copiado letras de músicas protegidas por direitos autorais para alimentar seus sistemas de treinamento, sem pagar pelo licenciamento.
Os autores também afirmam que a empresa armazenou cópias dessas composições em uma biblioteca interna, que poderia ser utilizada para desenvolver futuras versões do Claude.
Outro ponto envolve as respostas fornecidas pela inteligência artificial.
Segundo o Pitchfork, os representantes do catálogo alegam que o Claude conseguiu reproduzir estruturas e trechos de músicas protegidas quando recebeu pedidos para adaptá-las ao público moderno.
Em um dos exemplos apresentados pelos acusadores, o próprio chatbot teria reconhecido que suas versões permaneciam próximas das músicas originais, incluindo estruturas, refrões e versos.
A ação também acusa a Anthropic de remover informações que identificavam os titulares dos direitos autorais e de contornar mecanismos de proteção dos conteúdos.
Anthropic pode pagar mais de US$ 40 milhões
Os representantes das obras pedem até US$ 150 mil por música, o que representa US$ 41,1 milhões apenas pelas supostas violações de direitos autorais.
Entretanto, o valor total pode chegar a aproximadamente US$ 48,6 milhões, considerando os pedidos adicionais relacionados à remoção de informações de autoria e à violação de mecanismos de proteção.
Além da indenização, os autores solicitam que a Justiça impeça novas utilizações indevidas das obras e determine a eliminação de cópias não autorizadas.
Os valores correspondem aos pedidos apresentados no processo. Até o momento, não houve uma decisão judicial determinando que a Anthropic cometeu as infrações.
Procurada pelo Pitchfork, a empresa afirmou discordar das acusações e que pretende se defender integralmente.
Anthropic já enfrenta outros processos por direitos autorais
A disputa acontece em meio a outros processos que questionam o uso de materiais protegidos no treinamento de inteligência artificial.
Em 2023, editoras musicais como Universal Music Group, Concord e ABKCO já haviam acionado a Anthropic na Justiça, acusando o Claude de reproduzir letras sem autorização.
Na última quarta-feira (21), as partes discutiram o caso em uma audiência na Califórnia. Segundo a Reuters, a empresa defendeu que o treinamento de seus modelos pode ser protegido pelo conceito de fair use, previsto na legislação americana.
Esse princípio permite determinados usos de materiais protegidos sem autorização, dependendo das circunstâncias. A Anthropic argumenta que o treinamento transforma os conteúdos em uma tecnologia com finalidades diferentes das obras originais.
As editoras contestam essa interpretação e afirmam que a reprodução de letras por sistemas de IA pode prejudicar o mercado de músicas licenciadas.
A Justiça ainda não apresentou uma decisão sobre esse argumento no processo das editoras. O resultado poderá influenciar outras disputas envolvendo o treinamento de inteligência artificial com materiais protegidos por direitos autorais.

candidato.titulo: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
candidato.resumo: Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.

texto_fonte:
New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, News Bureau
- Summary:
- Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.
- Share:
Scientists have developed and tested the first three-dimensional thermal invisibility cloak, a device that can conceal objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme temperatures. The breakthrough could lead to new ways to cool microchips, safeguard delicate electronics, and prevent equipment from being detected through its thermal signature.
The cloak can conceal objects with a wide variety of shapes, regardless of the direction from which heat approaches. Earlier thermal cloaks were limited to two dimensions or worked only when heat traveled in a particular direction. The new design overcomes these restrictions by directing heat around a hidden object rather than simply blocking it. As a result, infrared imaging shows a temperature pattern that makes the object appear to be absent.
The research was conducted by University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign civil and environmental engineering professor Shelly Zhang, postdoctoral researcher Weichen Li, and graduate student Yibo Wang, in collaboration with professor Ole Sigmund of the Technical University of Denmark. Their findings were published in Nature Communications.
"A real thermal cloak should work no matter where the heat comes from," Zhang said. "Our device can hide a complex 3D object in an infinite number of directions while keeping the temperature inside stable and protected."
A New Material Makes 3D Thermal Invisibility Possible
Creating a thermal cloak that functions in three dimensions has been a longstanding challenge. Previous experimental devices could redirect heat only across a flat surface or along one direction of heat flow, leaving them far short of the capabilities needed for a fully three-dimensional cloak.
To overcome these limitations, the researchers revisited the foundational principles of transformation thermotics, a field that explores how heat can be redirected through specially designed materials. They focused on a central question: "What kind of material structure could cover almost all the thermal properties needed for a perfect cloak?"
The solution was a new lattice-based material whose structure can be independently adjusted along three directions. These changes allow the researchers to control how efficiently heat passes through different parts of the cloak. Compared with previous designs, the material can achieve a much broader range of thermal conductivities, closely approaching the properties predicted to be necessary for ideal thermal cloaking.
Importantly, the researchers went beyond computer simulations and constructed a working device. They used 3D metal printing to produce an intricate aluminum lattice, which provides pathways for efficient heat conduction. They then used mold casting to fill the remaining spaces with a rubber-like material that conducts heat poorly. Together, these materials create a structure that can carefully control the movement of heat.
Infrared Camera Tests Confirm the Cloak Works
To evaluate the device, the team positioned it between hot and cold regions, establishing a temperature difference that caused heat to flow through the surrounding environment. They monitored the resulting temperature patterns with an infrared camera to determine whether the cloak could successfully redirect heat around the concealed area.
The experiments showed that the device could guide heat around the hidden region while preserving the surrounding temperature pattern. To an infrared camera, the area appeared much as it would if no object were present. At the same time, temperatures inside the cloak remained uniform, shielding the concealed space from the extreme conditions outside.
The researchers also tested whether the cloak could accommodate unusually complicated objects. They successfully concealed intricate three-dimensional geometries, including detailed shapes resembling human heads. According to the team, earlier experimental thermal cloaks have not demonstrated a comparable combination of geometric complexity and cloaking performance.
Potential Applications in Electronics and Stealth Technology
The ability to control heat in three dimensions could have important implications across several industries. In electronics, the technology could help engineers direct heat away from sensitive components, improve thermal management in microchips, and protect devices operating under demanding conditions.
The researchers also see potential applications in security and defense. Future versions of the technology might help conceal people or equipment from thermal detection systems or shield valuable assets from severe temperature conditions. These uses would build on the device's demonstrated ability to redirect external heat while keeping the protected region thermally stable.
"Any field that needs precise control of heat or needs to protect something from being detected thermally could benefit from this work," Zhang said. "But we also see it more broadly: it's about hiding and protecting information that is carried by heat."
The Next Challenge Is Hiding Objects That Generate Heat
Although the current cloak represents a major advance, the researchers want to develop more sophisticated versions capable of performing additional functions. One particularly important goal is to conceal objects that produce heat themselves, rather than only protecting them from heat originating outside the cloak.
Achieving this would require materials that can actively control heat within the concealed region. Instead of simply redirecting incoming heat, a future cloak would need to concentrate, distribute, or guide thermal energy as conditions change. Such capabilities could expand the technology's usefulness in electronics, thermal protection, and applications involving infrared detection.
"We've shown that a true 3D omnidirectional thermal cloak is possible," Zhang said. "The next step is to make cloaks that don't just hide and protect, but also actively manipulate heat in useful ways."
The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Villum Foundation, and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. Zhang is also affiliated with mechanical science and engineering and the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
Journal Reference:
- Weichen Li, Yibo Wang, Ole Sigmund, Xiaojia Shelly Zhang. Free-form thermal cloaks in three dimensions. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-73167-0

candidato.titulo: CISA Unveils New Strategy to Strengthen National Cyber Defense and Critical Infrastructure Security

texto_fonte:
CISA Unveils New Strategy to Strengthen National Cyber Defense and Critical Infrastructure Security
WASHINGTON – The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) today released its new strategy, CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, which advances President Trump’s Cyber Strategy for America and National Resilience Strategy while strengthening the security and resilience of the nation’s critical infrastructure.
The strategy addresses an increasingly complex threat environment, strengthens national cyber defense, and prioritizes the infrastructure most essential to America’s national security, economy, public health, and safety.
The threat landscape is evolving at an unprecedented pace. Nation-state actors and other malicious adversaries are becoming increasingly sophisticated in their attempts to compromise U.S. networks. CISA is strengthening national cyber defense through decisive, proactive action to identify, disrupt, and eliminate adversarial access while hardening critical infrastructure against emerging threats.
“I call on every company and organization in the critical infrastructure community—from owners and operators to vendors and technology manufacturers—to act now,” said CISA Acting Director Nick Andersen. “CISA 2030 provides a focused roadmap to strengthen defenses, eliminate adversarial footholds, and deny them any advantage that could endanger the nation’s security, economy, or public health.”
CISA 2030 is guided by three pillars:
- Defend: Lead National Cyber Defense;
- Harden: Prioritize National Infrastructure Security, and
- Prevail: Mobilize National Resilience. Under the strategy, CISA will strengthen security across the interconnected physical and cyber dimensions of critical infrastructure.
The strategy also reaffirms CISA’s role, as delegated by the Department of Homeland Security, in leading the initiation and restoration of National Security and Emergency Preparedness communications, which are essential to maintaining continuity of government and public safety during crises.
The strategy recognizes that cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats increasingly intersect and can disrupt essential services Americans rely on every day. CISA will work with public- and private-sector partners to strengthen the security and resilience of operational technology, advance software security, support secure emerging technologies, and improve continuity of National Security and Emergency Preparedness communications.
In alignment with Cyber Strategy for America, CISA will move from a passive defense posture toward an aggressive, anticipatory stance focused on identifying, mitigating, and reducing malicious access to critical infrastructure. The agency will also improve its ability to prioritize risk, mobilize partners, and support rapid, coordinated action when threats emerge.
The strategy sets out CISA’s priorities for the coming year:
- Within 60 days, CISA will begin reviewing its core services and capabilities to meet key objectives.
- Within 180 days, CISA will provide a plan to implement the strategy and measure its results.
- Within 365 days, CISA will report on its progress in carrying out the strategy.
CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail delivers a clear, decisive roadmap for advancing the agency’s mission and strengthening the security and resilience of the nation’s critical infrastructure in service to the American people.
###
About CISA
As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.
Visit CISA.gov for more information and follow us on X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram.
